title: Retro notes — Hardware tuning profiles pack v1 (runtime-1.22) launch
content:
Context
- v1 “Hardware tuning profiles pack” shipped as part of runtime-1.22. Default enablement via feature flag in Hosted canary cohort, Dedicated opt-in, Private available via Helm/installer values.
- SKUs in scope: H100 + L40S (B200 gated / explicit version required).
- This retro is focused on the launch process + early operational behavior, not a deep kernel perf postmortem.

When / attendees
- Date: 2026-02-20
- Notes owner: Talia
- Attendees: Mateo, Noah, Hiro, Sofia, Omar, Sean, Rafael, Allison, Connor, Lauren (partial)

What we set out to do (success definition we used in go/no-go)
- Zero-sev incident attributable to profile defaults.
- No sustained regression vs baseline on p95/p99 for mixed workloads in canary; any regression must be observable + reversible quickly.
- Profile version + id visible in logs + health/debug endpoint.
- Bench results tied to profile_version; perf-canary would catch “obvious” regressions on default changes.

What went well
1) Versioning + observability paid off immediately
- Having profile_id + sku tags on latency histograms + scheduler_queue_ms made the canary review 10x easier than past runtime perf launches.
- /health + debug endpoint including profile_version reduced on-call back-and-forth (no more “what config is this pool actually running?”).
- Kernel choice metric/counter was especially useful for confirming that H100 kernel v3 was being used where expected and not silently falling back.

2) Clear separation of “fleet default” vs “customer pin” reduced scope creep
- The guardrails around overrides prevented a bunch of “quick fix” suggestions that would have been unsafe (e.g., turning down headroom or raising concurrency on L40S just to hit a throughput number).
- Dedicated opt-in stance kept pressure off SRE during the Hosted canary week.

3) Rollout choreography was disciplined
- Connor’s checklist (docs readiness + gating + backout) forced us to close a lot of small gaps before enabling the canary.
- Kill-switch semantics were actually exercised in staging and we validated rollback behavior end-to-end.

4) Benchmark-lab integration is “good enough” for v1
- Being able to point to benchmark-lab runs tagged with profile_version + git sha helped align runtime vs infra vs product when discussing expected performance.
- We still have noise issues (see below) but the pipeline exists and is getting used.

5) Cross-team collaboration worked (esp. SRE + Observability)
- Allison’s team helped keep metric names/labels consistent; cardinality concerns were raised early enough to avoid late rewrites.
- Sean/Rafael pushed on “what pages vs what tickets” and we ended up with reasonable initial alerting instead of paging on everything.

What didn’t go well / pain points
1) We still shipped one bad default (batching) and had to hotfix
- The “aggressive batching default” change increased p99 latency on a mixed prompt-length workload in Hosted canary.
- We had the visibility to see it quickly, but it still made it to canary. Hotfix PR reverted it.
- Root cause (tentative): workload bucket classification undercounted long-prefill mix; queue policy was starving long-prefill requests under high concurrency; batching amplified the tail.
- Takeaway: perf-canary needs to better represent mixed + long-prefill cases, and acceptance thresholds should include a hard p99 delta cap for mixed buckets.

2) L40S stability is fragile under burst traffic (OOM/fragmentation)
- We saw intermittent OOMs in L40S pool under bursty load patterns (not catastrophic, but enough to open/support tickets and force a workaround).
- Observed: fragmentation estimate trending up + compaction time spikes right before OOM in the affected pool.
- We did have headroom settings, but they were not conservative enough for the “burst + mixed prompts + high churn” scenario.
- Takeaway: L40S profile defaults need to bias for stability (headroom + concurrency cap + stricter admission control) even if it costs some throughput.

3) Compatibility matrix / fleet heterogeneity documentation was scattered
- Infra asked the same question multiple times: “which driver/CUDA combos are we truly supporting per profile version?”
- We had partial answers in PR descriptions + Slack threads; not centralized enough.
- Takeaway: produce a single compatibility table per profile pack version (even if it is short) and link it everywhere.

4) Too much “tribal knowledge” around workload buckets
- The bucket definitions exist in code + bench harness, but the human-readable explanation is weak.
- Product/CS couldn’t easily translate “bucket X” into what the customer sees (short chats vs long-context summarization, etc.).

5) We underestimated the operational need for a “profile diff” view
- During the p99 regression triage, everyone wanted: “what changed between v1.0.0 and v1.0.1?” (knob-by-knob).
- We had git diffs but they are noisy and not easily consumable in an incident.
- Takeaway: generate an automated changelog/diff artifact for profile packs (even basic: changed fields + defaults).

What broke / incidents / customer impact (early signals)
- Hosted canary (H100):
  - One tail-latency regression detected in canary cohort; reverted batching default (hotfix). No broad outage.
  - No major error-rate regressions tied to profile pack itself.
- Dedicated (H100):
  - One customer ticket reporting higher p99 post-upgrade; mitigated by pinning profile version / reverting to prior defaults. Still an uncomfortable escalation.
  - Takeaway: Dedicated comms need to explicitly mention pin/rollback as a supported short-term mitigation and provide steps.
- L40S (Hosted + some Dedicated pools):
  - Intermittent OOM reports under burst; workaround was reducing concurrency cap / increasing headroom; follow-up change queued.

Metrics / dashboards (what we watched, what was missing)
What we watched and it helped
- p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency by profile_id + model + route
- scheduler_queue_ms (queueing separated from compute time)
- kernel_choice + kernel_fallback counters for H100
- KV cache compaction time + fragmentation estimate (very actionable)
- GPU memory watermark vs headroom target

What was missing / too hard to interpret
- A single “SLO gate summary” view (one page) that says: are we within rollout guardrails right now?
- Better correlation between admission control decisions and tail latency (e.g., “requests rejected due to queue limit” overlaid with p99).
- Better attribution for “fallback happened” (why: long context? unsupported shape? driver mismatch? memory pressure?)

Process notes (release / coordination)
- Good: go/no-go thread forced explicit sign-offs; we had a clear canary cohort definition.
- Bad: doc review timing was too late; some expected behavior tables were still WIP when we were already doing canary review.
- Suggestion: treat docs readiness as a first-class gating item (like tests). If tables aren’t done, we don’t enable canary.

What we should keep doing
- Profile selection logic in runtime with explicit precedence (fleet default -> deploy override -> customer pin) + audit logging.
- Hard compatibility gates for “new” SKUs (B200 approach is correct): refuse unsafe defaults, require explicit profile version.
- Feature-flagged rollout with kill switch + pre-agreed rollback steps.

Follow-ups for v1.1 (proposed)
P0 (must do before expanding default rollout)
- L40S stability defaults:
  - Increase KV/memory headroom target.
  - Reduce default concurrency cap for the mixed bucket.
  - Tighten admission control thresholds on L40S to prevent “burst to OOM”.
  - Add clearer runbook guidance: symptoms + immediate mitigation steps.
- Perf-canary + benchmark matrix:
  - Add a mixed workload bucket with long-prefill + short-decode skew.
  - Add explicit p99 guardrail thresholds for mixed buckets; fail closed for default changes.
  - Reduce noise by standardizing run ordering + warmup + seed handling (Rina to propose).
- Profile pack “diff/changelog” artifact:
  - Auto-generate a knob-by-knob diff between versions (human readable).
  - Store alongside benchmark artifacts.

P1 (should do)
- Compatibility documentation:
  - Single compatibility matrix per profile_version (SKU x driver x CUDA x MIG policy assumptions).
  - Link from release notes + on-call runbook + Private installer warnings.
- Workload buckets documentation:
  - Translate bucket names into customer-relevant scenarios.
  - Make it obvious which bucket a live request is landing in (log field / trace tag).
- Improve fallback attribution:
  - Add “fallback_reason” enum counter for kernel fallback.
  - Add “profile_guardrail_triggered” counters for override rejection / clamp events.

P2 (nice-to-have)
- Console UX:
  - Show active profile_id/profile_version in debugging view (in a way support can screenshot).
  - A ‘copy debug bundle’ action that includes profile + key knob values.
- Extend to additional shapes/models:
  - Add explicit profiles for ultra-long context (where kernel fallbacks + memory pressure are expected).

Open questions
- Do we want semantic-ish versioning for profiles (v1.0.0 etc.) to be “API stability” or just “pack revision”? Today it’s sort of both.
- For Dedicated: do we default to “pinned until customer opts into latest” or “track latest within a major/minor”? Needs product + SRE alignment.
- How strict should override guardrails be for Private customers (where they control hardware variance)? Probably keep strict defaults but allow an escape hatch with explicit acknowledgement + audit.

Action items (owners + rough dates; to be filed in Linear)
- Sofia + Marcus: propose v1.1 mixed-bucket definition + acceptance thresholds (target: 2026-03-06)
- Omar + Samir: L40S headroom/concurrency proposal + tests (target: 2026-03-08)
- Allison: SLO gate summary dashboard panel spec (target: 2026-03-01)
- Quentin: compatibility matrix template per profile_version (target: 2026-03-04)
- Connor: profile pack changelog/diff generation in release process (target: 2026-03-11)
- Lauren: Dedicated customer comms update to include pin/rollback steps + expectation framing (target: 2026-03-05)

Notes to self / parking lot
- We should write down the “kill switch muscle memory” explicitly (who can trigger, what it reverts, where audit trail lands) because we got lucky that the right people were around during the canary.
- Consider a “profile safety score” output at startup (green/yellow/red) based on detected driver/CUDA + headroom + concurrency; might help Private installs.
